STI Awareness: Protecting Your Sexual Health

Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections that can be passed between people through sexual contact. Some STIs cause noticeable symptoms, while others may cause few or no symptoms at all. This means a person can have an infection without knowing it, making prevention and testing important parts of sexual healthcare.

STI awareness is not only about avoiding infection. It is about having reliable information, knowing how to reduce risk, recognizing when testing may be appropriate, and understanding where to seek confidential healthcare.

Reduce the Risk of STIs

Different infections spread in different ways, so no single prevention method covers every situation.

Prevention may include using condoms or other barrier methods correctly, getting recommended vaccinations such as HPV and hepatitis B vaccines, having open conversations with partners about sexual health, and accessing regular STI testing when appropriate.

Some infections can be prevented or treated with additional medical options. A healthcare professional or sexual-health clinic can explain which prevention strategies are appropriate based on an individual's circumstances.

Testing Matters—Even Without Symptoms

It is possible to have an STI and feel completely well. Testing can identify infections earlier and allow treatment or follow-up before complications develop or an infection is unknowingly passed to someone else.

Testing may be considered after a possible exposure, when beginning a new sexual relationship, when a partner has been diagnosed with an STI, or when recommended by a healthcare provider.

STI testing can involve different types of samples depending on the infection being tested for. A healthcare provider can explain which tests are appropriate and when they should be completed.

If You Notice a Change

Unusual changes or concerns related to sexual health should be discussed with a healthcare professional rather than diagnosed from symptoms alone. Many symptoms can have causes unrelated to an STI, and some STIs have no symptoms.

Family doctors, nurse practitioners and sexual-health clinics can provide testing, treatment, vaccination, prevention information and guidance about notifying partners when necessary.

Sexual Health Care Should Be Confidential and Respectful

For newcomers and young people, concerns about privacy, cultural expectations or embarrassment can make it harder to ask questions about sexual health.

Sexual healthcare is healthcare. Patients can ask what information will remain confidential, what a test involves, why it is recommended and what the results mean. Healthcare providers can also discuss prevention without assuming a person's relationship status, background or sexual experience.

Know Before You Need Care

Knowing where sexual-health services are available makes it easier to seek care when needed. The goal is informed decision-making: understand how infections are transmitted, reduce preventable risks, test when appropriate and seek healthcare without stigma.

Protection and Prevention for Youth & Young Adults

Taking care of sexual health means having accurate information and knowing how to reduce preventable risks. For teens and young adults, this includes understanding consent, preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs), preventing unintended pregnancy, and knowing when and where to seek healthcare.

Know How to Protect Yourself

Use protection consistently. Condoms and other barrier methods can reduce the risk of many STIs when used correctly.

Condoms can also help prevent pregnancy. Other birth-control methods may prevent pregnancy but do not necessarily protect against STIs.

Protection and Prevention for Youth & Young Adults

Taking care of sexual health means having accurate information and knowing how to reduce preventable risks. For teens and young adults, this includes understanding consent, preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs), preventing unintended pregnancy, and knowing when and where to seek healthcare.

Know How to Protect Yourself

Use protection consistently. Condoms and other barrier methods can reduce the risk of many STIs when used correctly.

Condoms can also help prevent pregnancy. Other birth-control methods may prevent pregnancy but do not necessarily protect against STIs.

Learn about vaccination. Vaccines can prevent some infections that may be transmitted through sexual contact, including HPV and hepatitis B. A healthcare provider can help determine which vaccines are recommended based on age and vaccination history.

Consider STI testing. Some STIs may have no noticeable symptoms. Testing is an important way to know your status and receive treatment when needed. A healthcare provider or sexual-health clinic can advise when testing is appropriate.

Talk about sexual health. Conversations about boundaries, protection, contraception and STI testing can be part of healthy relationships. Decisions should be made without pressure, and everyone involved has the right to set or change their boundaries.

Use reliable health information. Social media, friends and online forums can contain misleading sexual-health information. For questions about contraception, STI prevention, testing or symptoms, use trusted public-health resources or speak with a qualified healthcare professional.

Remember: Pregnancy and STI Prevention Are Different

A method that prevents pregnancy may not protect against STIs. Birth-control options such as the pill, implant or intrauterine device (IUD) are designed primarily to prevent pregnancy, while condoms can also reduce the risk of many STIs.

A healthcare professional can explain available options and help someone understand which approach is appropriate for their needs.

Know Where to Get Support

Sexual-health questions are healthcare questions. Youth and young adults can seek information and services from family doctors, nurse practitioners, sexual-health clinics, community health centres, pharmacies and other appropriate health services.

Depending on the service and location, support may include contraception information, STI testing and treatment, vaccination, pregnancy testing and sexual-health education.

If privacy is a concern, ask the healthcare provider to explain how confidentiality works and whether there are any limits before sharing personal information.

Make Informed Choices

Protection and prevention are not about fear or judgment. They are about having enough information to make decisions about your health.

Know your options. Ask questions. Respect boundaries. Use appropriate protection. Get tested when recommended. Seek healthcare when you need it.

Birth Control Options for Youth & Young Adults

Birth control, also called contraception, helps prevent pregnancy. There are several options, and the best choice can depend on health needs, how often the method needs to be used, personal preference, cost and access to healthcare.

Understanding the differences can help young people ask informed questions when speaking with a healthcare provider.

Condoms

Condoms are used during sexual activity to help prevent pregnancy. They also provide protection against many sexually transmitted infections (STIs), which makes them different from most other birth-control methods.

Birth Control Pills

Birth control pills contain hormones that help prevent pregnancy and are taken on a regular schedule. Different types of pills are available, and a healthcare provider can help determine whether they are appropriate based on a person's health and medical history.

Important: Birth control pills do not protect against STIs.

IUD — Intrauterine Device

An IUD is a small device placed in the uterus by a healthcare professional. Hormonal and non-hormonal options are available, and depending on the type, an IUD can provide pregnancy prevention for several years.

Emergency Contraception

Emergency contraception can help prevent pregnancy after unprotected sexual activity or when another birth-control method did not work as intended.

Options include emergency contraceptive pills and, in some circumstances, certain IUDs. Because timing and suitability can vary, a pharmacist or healthcare provider can provide guidance about available options.

Emergency contraception is intended to prevent pregnancy; it does not end an established pregnancy and does not protect against STIs.

Choosing a Birth Control Method

There is no single birth-control method that is right for everyone. A healthcare provider or pharmacist can explain effectiveness, possible side effects, STI protection, cost and how each method is accessed.

It is also important to remember that most birth-control methods prevent pregnancy but do not prevent STIs. Condoms can help reduce the risk of many STIs and may be used alongside another contraceptive method.

Learning about contraception is part of understanding sexual health. Young people can ask questions, discuss their options with a healthcare professional and make informed decisions about their health and boundaries.

Gender Identity and Inclusivity

Canada is home to people with different cultures, identities, families and life experiences. In healthcare, everyone should be treated with dignity and respect and have access to care without discrimination.

Understanding gender identity and inclusive healthcare can help newcomers and young people communicate more comfortably with healthcare providers and understand what respectful care should look like.

Understanding Gender Identity

Gender identity refers to a person's internal sense of their gender. A person may identify as a woman, man, non-binary, or another gender. Gender identity is different from biological characteristics and from sexual orientation.

People may express their gender through clothing, names, pronouns or other aspects of their appearance and everyday life. Not everyone expresses or experiences gender in the same way.

What Does Inclusive Healthcare Mean?

Inclusive healthcare recognizes that patients have different identities, cultures, languages and experiences.

In practice, this can mean healthcare providers:

communicate respectfully and avoid assumptions about a patient's identity or relationships; use the patient's name and pronouns appropriately; explain examinations, tests and treatment before proceeding; provide relevant health information based on the person's individual needs; respect privacy and confidentiality within applicable rules; and provide care without judgment or discrimination.

Patients can also ask questions if they do not understand why personal information is being requested or how it relates to their healthcare.

Respect Works Both Ways

Inclusive communities do not require everyone to have the same experiences, beliefs or cultural background. They do require people to treat one another with dignity.

For newcomers, some language or conversations around gender may be unfamiliar. Learning what terms mean can make it easier to understand healthcare forms, school information and conversations with healthcare professionals without requiring someone to already know every term.

Understanding Public Health in Canada

Public health is the part of the health system that works to prevent illness, promote well-being and protect communities. While doctors and clinics often focus on the health needs of individual patients, public health looks at health concerns that can affect families, neighbourhoods and entire communities.

For someone new to Canada, public health may already be part of everyday life. Vaccination programs, food inspections, school health services, drinking-water advisories, disease outbreak notices and information about extreme weather or air quality are all examples of public health in action.

Public Health Protects Communities

Public health helps identify and respond to health risks before they affect more people. Health authorities monitor concerns such as infectious diseases, food and water safety, environmental hazards and other issues that may affect community health.

When necessary, public-health authorities may issue alerts or recommendations so people know what is happening and what precautions to take.

Prevention Helps Reduce Illness

Preventing illness is a major part of public health. Vaccination, screening, infection prevention, safe food practices and early detection can help reduce the spread of disease and identify health concerns earlier.

Newcomers who have vaccination records from another country should keep them and bring them when accessing healthcare. A healthcare provider or public-health professional can review the records and identify whether additional vaccines are recommended.

Health Education Improves Well-being

Public health also helps people make informed decisions about their health. Programs may provide information about nutrition, physical activity, sexual health, pregnancy, child development, mental well-being, substance use, disease prevention and environmental health.

Reliable health information can be especially useful when adjusting to a healthcare system that works differently from the one you are familiar with.

Everyone Plays a Role in Community Health

Public health is a shared effort. Everyday actions—such as following food-safety practices, staying up to date with recommended vaccinations, following public-health advisories and taking appropriate steps to prevent the spread of infections—can help protect both individuals and the people around them.

Community health is also shaped by access to safe housing, clean water, nutritious food, education, healthcare and supportive environments. Public health works with communities and other services to address these broader influences on health.

Key Points to Remember

Public health protects communities by identifying health risks and supporting safer environments. Prevention helps reduce illness through measures such as vaccination, screening and infection prevention.

Health education improves well-being by giving people reliable information to make informed health decisions.

Everyone plays a role in community health through individual actions, community participation and shared responsibility for healthier environments.

Understanding public health can help newcomers recognize important health information, know when an advisory applies to them and make better use of the programs and services available in their community.

Vaccines and Immunization in Canada

Vaccines help protect people from serious infectious diseases by preparing the immune system to recognize and respond to specific infections. Immunization is an important part of preventive healthcare in Canada and is recommended at different stages of life, from childhood through adulthood.

For newcomers, vaccination recommendations in Canada may differ from those in another country. Previous vaccination records can help healthcare providers determine which vaccines have already been received and whether any additional doses are recommended.

What Do Vaccines Protect Against?

Vaccines are available for a range of preventable diseases. Depending on a person's age, health, vaccination history and other factors, recommended vaccines may include protection against: Influenza (flu) — vaccination is recommended regularly because circulating influenza viruses can change over time.

COVID-19 — vaccination recommendations are updated as public-health guidance and available vaccines change.

Measles — a highly contagious infection that can cause serious complications. Protection is commonly provided through combination vaccines such as MMR.

Hepatitis — vaccines are available against hepatitis A and hepatitis B. Recommendations depend on factors such as age, previous immunization and risk.

Tetanus — protection is usually provided as part of combination vaccines, with booster doses recommended at certain times.

HPV (Human Papillomavirus) — vaccination helps protect against HPV infections that can lead to several types of cancer and other health conditions.

New to Canada? Check Your Immunization Record

If you have vaccination records from your home country, keep them and bring them to a healthcare provider or public-health clinic. Even if the record uses different vaccine names or schedules, it may help determine your vaccination history.

If records are unavailable or incomplete, a healthcare professional can explain what steps may be appropriate rather than assuming that every vaccination needs to be restarted.

Are Vaccines Free in Canada?

Many recommended vaccines are publicly funded, meaning eligible people can receive them without paying directly. However, coverage varies by province or territory, age, health needs and the vaccine being provided.

Vaccines may be available through public-health clinics, family doctors, pharmacies, schools or other healthcare services, depending on where you live.

Key Points

Vaccines help prevent disease. Immunization reduces the risk of many vaccine-preventable illnesses and their complications.

Immunization protects communities. When more people are protected against an infection, there are fewer opportunities for some diseases to spread, which can also help protect people who are more vulnerable.

Some vaccines are provided free in Canada. Publicly funded vaccines vary across provinces and territories, so check the immunization program where you live.

Speak with a healthcare provider about vaccines. A doctor, nurse, pharmacist or public-health professional can review your vaccination history and explain which vaccines are recommended for you.

Keeping an immunization record and checking provincial recommendations can make it easier to stay up to date as you settle in Canada.

Understanding Communicable Diseases

Communicable diseases are illnesses caused by infectious organisms such as viruses, bacteria, fungi or parasites that can spread between people or through contaminated food, water, surfaces, animals or insects.

Knowing how an infection spreads is important because the precautions needed for one disease may be different from another. Public-health guidance, vaccination, hygiene and early healthcare can all help reduce the spread of infection within families and communities.

Understand the Types of Communicable Diseases

Communicable diseases can be grouped by how they are transmitted. Respiratory infections can spread through infectious particles released when people breathe, talk, cough or sneeze. Examples include influenza, COVID-19 and tuberculosis.

Food- and water-borne infections can occur when food or water becomes contaminated. Examples include norovirus, salmonellosis and hepatitis A.

Direct-contact infections can spread through close contact with an infected person or, for some infections, contaminated objects or surfaces. Examples include certain skin infections.

Vector-borne diseases are transmitted by organisms such as mosquitoes and ticks. Examples include Lyme disease and West Nile virus, both of which occur in Canada.

Blood and body-fluid infections can spread through specific exposures to infected blood or other body fluids. Examples include hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.

Safety Measures Against Infection

Prevention depends on how a particular infection spreads. Everyday measures such as washing hands thoroughly, following safe food-handling practices, covering coughs and sneezes, and avoiding close contact with others when sick can reduce the spread of many infections.

Vaccination also provides protection against several communicable diseases. Other precautions may include using insect repellent and checking for ticks, practising safer sex, and avoiding the sharing of personal items that could be contaminated with blood.

During an outbreak, local public-health authorities may recommend additional precautions based on the disease and level of risk.

Necessary Safety Precautions

Knowing when to act is just as important as knowing how infections spread. Pay attention to public-health notices, food recalls, vaccination recommendations and local disease advisories.

If you develop symptoms or know you have been exposed to an infectious disease, contact an appropriate healthcare service for guidance. Depending on the infection, you may be advised to stay home, get tested, receive treatment or take additional precautions around other people.

Extra care may be needed around people who are more likely to become seriously ill from certain infections, including infants, older adults and some people with underlying health conditions.

Follow-Up and Treatment

Treatment is different for every communicable disease. Some infections improve with supportive care, while others require specific medicines or ongoing medical follow-up. Antibiotics treat certain bacterial infections, but they do not treat viral infections such as influenza.

If treatment is prescribed, follow the healthcare provider's instructions and attend recommended follow-up appointments. Follow-up may be used to check recovery, review test results, manage complications or determine whether additional testing or treatment is needed.

Some communicable diseases must also be reported to public health. In these situations, public-health professionals may contact the person to provide guidance and identify whether others may have been exposed.

Key Points

Understand how diseases spread. Different communicable diseases require different prevention measures.

Use the right safety measures. Vaccination, hygiene, safe food practices and other precautions can reduce the risk of infection.

Respond appropriately when illness occurs. Follow public-health guidance and take precautions to reduce spreading an infection to others.

Complete treatment and follow-up. Seek healthcare when needed, follow treatment instructions and attend recommended follow-up appointments.

Understanding Seasonal Health Risks in Canada

Canada experiences four distinct seasons—winter, spring, summer and fall—but weather conditions vary considerably across the country. Temperatures can shift from extreme cold in winter to periods of intense heat in summer, while changes in air quality, allergens, insects and infectious diseases can also occur throughout the year.

For newcomers, understanding these seasonal changes makes it easier to prepare for the weather and recognize health risks that may be unfamiliar.

Winter: Extreme Cold, Snow and Ice

Canadian winters can bring freezing temperatures, heavy snowfall, strong winds and icy conditions. Exposure to extreme cold can lead to cold-related illness, while snow and ice increase the risk of slips, falls and transportation difficulties.

Dress in warm layers and use appropriate winter clothing, including insulated footwear, gloves or mittens and head covering. Check weather warnings before travelling and limit prolonged exposure during extreme cold.

Winter is also associated with increased circulation of respiratory infections such as influenza. Following current vaccination recommendations, washing hands regularly and taking appropriate precautions when sick can help reduce transmission.

Spring: Allergies, Changing Weather and Ticks

Spring temperatures can change quickly as warmer weather returns. Pollen from trees and other plants may trigger seasonal allergies, causing symptoms such as sneezing, congestion and irritated or watery eyes.

Ticks also become more active as temperatures rise. When spending time in wooded, grassy or brush-covered areas, use appropriate insect protection and check clothing, skin and pets for ticks afterward.

Summer: Heat, Sun and Air Quality

Periods of high temperatures can increase the risk of heat-related illness, particularly during heat waves. Staying hydrated, reducing strenuous activity during the hottest part of the day and spending time in cooler environments can help manage heat exposure.

Sun protection is also important. Shade, suitable clothing and sunscreen can reduce exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

Wildfire smoke and poor air quality can affect some Canadian communities during warmer months. Check local air-quality information and follow public-health advice when smoke or other air-quality concerns are present.

Fall: Cooler Weather and Respiratory Illness

Fall brings shorter days and gradually cooler temperatures. It is also a useful time to prepare for winter and check seasonal health recommendations.

Respiratory infections often become more common during the colder months. Public-health authorities may provide updated recommendations for seasonal vaccines, including influenza and COVID-19 vaccination.

Having appropriate winter clothing and basic emergency supplies ready before severe winter weather begins can also make the transition into winter easier.

Managing Seasonal Health Risks

Canada's weather can change quickly, so preparation should begin before conditions become severe. Check local forecasts and weather alerts, dress for current conditions and learn which health risks are common in your region.

Seasonal health management may include vaccination, hydration, sun protection, insect and tick protection, appropriate clothing, monitoring air quality and preparing for extreme weather.

Health risks also vary between provinces and communities. Local public-health authorities and Environment and Climate Change Canada provide regional information when extreme weather or environmental conditions may affect health.

Safety During Extreme Weather in Canada

Canada's weather can change quickly, and some conditions can become dangerous. Depending on where you live, you may experience winter storms, extreme cold, heat waves, thunderstorms, flooding, wildfire smoke or other severe weather events.

For newcomers who have not experienced these conditions before, knowing what to expect and preparing ahead of time can reduce health and safety risks.

Extreme Cold and Winter Storms

Winter storms can bring very low temperatures, heavy snow, strong winds, freezing rain and poor visibility. Severe weather can also disrupt transportation and, occasionally, electricity or other services.

Cold exposure can lead to serious health problems, while snow and ice increase the risk of falls and injuries.

During extreme cold:

Check the weather forecast and warnings before leaving home. Dress in several warm layers and protect exposed skin with appropriate winter clothing.

Wear insulated, slip-resistant footwear when conditions are icy. Limit unnecessary time outdoors during extreme cold or severe storms.

Keep basic supplies at home in case travel becomes difficult. Avoid unnecessary travel when authorities advise people to stay off the roads.

If someone develops concerning symptoms after prolonged cold exposure, move indoors and seek appropriate medical help.

Heat Waves and Extreme Heat

Canadian summers can also include periods of very high temperatures and humidity. During a heat wave, the body may have difficulty cooling itself, increasing the risk of heat-related illness.

Stay hydrated throughout the day and spend time in air-conditioned or cooler spaces when possible. Reduce strenuous outdoor activity during the hottest parts of the day and never leave children, pets or other vulnerable people inside a parked vehicle.

Pay particular attention to local heat warnings and check on family members or others who may have difficulty managing extreme heat.

Wildfire Smoke and Poor Air Quality

Wildfire smoke can travel long distances and affect air quality even in communities far from the fire itself. Smoke can irritate the eyes and respiratory system and may affect some people more severely.

When air quality is poor, check local air-quality information and follow public-health recommendations. This may include reducing strenuous outdoor activity or spending more time indoors when smoke levels are high.

Storms, Flooding and Power Outages

Severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, flooding and high winds can create additional risks. Avoid flooded roads and areas, stay away from downed power lines and follow evacuation or emergency instructions from local authorities.

Power outages can also affect heating, cooling, food storage and medical equipment. Keeping a basic emergency kit with essentials such as water, non-perishable food, a flashlight, batteries and necessary medications can help households manage short disruptions.
